Local LLMs on AMD Strix Halo (Ryzen AI MAX+ 395) on Linux#

The AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395, codenamed Strix Halo, puts a Radeon 8060S iGPU (gfx1151), an XDNA 2 NPU and 128 GB of memory shared between them in one machine. The 1bit engine is built for that one chip: it serves local LLMs on its GPU and its NPU, on Linux, behind the OpenAI-compatible API of AMD's Lemonade Server. This page gathers what the docs and the posts say about running local LLMs on it, with a link to where each fact is measured.

The GPU: Radeon 8060S through HRX#

The engine's one GPU route is HRX: AMD's ggml-hrx with its Loom kernels, plus our own HIP kernels, in one llama.cpp build. HRX runs every graph node of every model and mode we test on the Strix Halo GPU: 43 of 43 configurations in the 2026-10-20 census, with 0 nodes on the CPU (HRX, Every node on the GPU). Every ggml weight type runs on it, including NVFP4, Q2_0, MXFP4 and the ternary TQ, PTQ and PQ formats, so any GGUF quantization loads, from Unsloth's dynamic quants to BitNet b1.58.

The NPU: XDNA 2 on Linux#

The NPU engine runs models on the XDNA 2 NPU on Linux, on our own runtime and kernels. It is in progress, correctness first and speed next; Qwen3-0.6B decodes at 88.6 tok/s on it in the release gate. The NPU and the GPU were measured running at the same time, forty repetitions with no hang and no corruption (the measurement), and the hybrid route puts the prompt on one device and the generated tokens on the other. PrismML's ternary Bonsai-2-27B already answers correctly on the NPU (Ternary Bonsai on the NPU).

Measured on the machine#

Every number below was taken on a Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 at the current pins; the full table, and how each number is taken, are on Models measured and How we measure.

model route measured
Qwen3.8-27B, UD-Q4_K_XL HRX decode 36.0 tok/s with MTP on code prompts; 56.6 tok/s with the DFlash2 drafter
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (MoE) HRX prefill 287 tok/s, decode 24.0 tok/s
Zyphra ZAYA1-8B, Q4_K_M HRX decode 157 tok/s
PrismML Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B, PQ2_0 HRX decode 43.3 tok/s with MTP
Microsoft BitNet b1.58 2B-4T, TQ2_0 HRX decode 123.4 tok/s
Qwen3-0.6B NPU decode 88.6 tok/s in the release gate

Speculative decoding pays on the dense models: the model's own MTP head, or a separate drafter such as DFlash2, guesses several tokens that the model checks in one pass. On Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, a MoE already at 88 tok/s, every draft model we tried was slower (Speculative decoding: where it pays).

Lemonade Server and the OpenAI API#

The engine runs inside Lemonade as its onebit backend, and that recipe passes Lemonade's own LLM test suite on HRX: 31 of 31 tests run, all pass. Lemonade is what you talk to, with its catalog, downloads, router and web UI; 1bit serve exposes nothing but an OpenAI-compatible API, so any OpenAI client works with it. On Ubuntu 26.04 the engine plugs into the stock lemond from Lemonade's PPA.

Ways to run it#

  • 1bit OS from a USB stick: Lemonade Server with the engine inside, on a stick that boots the machine with Secure Boot on; 1bit-install puts the same system on a disk (1bit OS, Boot a stick).
  • On an Ubuntu that already runs Lemonade: the lemonade-onebit package adds the engine as a Lemonade backend (Lemonade).

Both ship on the releases page when a release has passed its checklist (Releases). The source is Apache-2.0 on GitHub; questions are answered in the FAQ.
